title: PulseCare POC scoping - quality eval plan
next_steps: Redwood: share initial quality evaluation template and golden prompt set (by 2025-10-17)
PulseCare: send sample corpus and PII redaction requirements (by 2025-10-20)
Schedule benchmark run: Redwood to propose 2 windows for 5k-token throughput test
action_items: Jordan Park: upload quality eval spreadsheet and scoring rubric to shared drive; due 2025-10-17
Ethan Li: provide 2 weeks of anonymized transcripts and a schema for expected output formats; due 2025-10-20
Lina Gomez: set up baseline hosted model bench and send results; due 2025-10-24
summary: POC scoping focused on quality evaluation plan for PulseCare's clinical summarization use-case. Discussed golden prompts, regression tests, hallucination detection, format compliance checks, scoring rules, sampling strategy, and timeline for benchmark runs. Agreement to exchange sample data and an initial eval spreadsheet; next benchmark to run on Redwood hosted endpoints before considering Dedicated or Private deployment.
transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Park: Hey everyone, thanks for making time. Jordan from Redwood here, with Lina the SE. Quick roll call?
[00:06] Rajiv Patel: Rajiv here, head of data at PulseCare. Sofia and Ethan on.
[00:10] Sofia Moreno: Hi all.
[00:12] Lina Gomez: Lina, Redwood SE. Good to meet you.
[00:15] Jordan Park: Cool. Today we want to scope the POC and nail down the quality evaluation plan - golden prompts, regression, hallucination checks, format checks, scoring. Roughly 45 minutes. Sound good?
[00:24] Ethan Li: Yep sounds good. we're mainly doing clinical note summarization, and we need tight format outputs for downstream systems.
[00:31] Jordan Park: Excellent. Can you walk us through the success criteria from your side, Rajiv or Sofia?
[00:36] Rajiv Patel: Sure. Primary success is format compliance - our EHR ingest requires JSON with keys diagnosis, plan, follow_up. Need at least 95% exact key presence and minimal schema drift. Secondary is factuality: low hallucination on meds and allergies, ideally under 2% hallucination for critical fields. Latency also matters: avg generation under 1.2s for 512 tokens, but that's later.
[01:03] Sofia Moreno: And from product we'd like high end-user satisfaction on summaries, we plan a small clinician QA in week two of the pilot.
[01:10] Lina Gomez: Helpful. For format checks we usually do schema validation and then token-level regex/templating to catch malformed dates and units. For hallucination we can run entity grounding where the model output is checked against the source text for extracted entities.
[01:23] Ethan Li: Can you expand on the grounding approach? Sounds like NER + exact-match?
[01:27] Lina Gomez: Right, we extract medication and allergy mentions from the source, then verify if the summary asserts the same meds and that any new meds are flagged as "not in source". We also do a non-overlap check - if model asserts a diagnosis not supported by source, it's a hallucination. Not perfect, but it flags high-risk errors for human review.
[01:44] Jordan Park: On scoring, we propose a hybrid approach: automated pass/fail for format and critical entity checks; continuous numeric metrics for semantic quality (BERTScore / embedding similarity) and a sampled human rater score for clinical usefulness. Weighted scoring: 40% format/facts pass rate, 40% semantic similarity, 20% human rating.
[02:02] Rajiv Patel: Hmm the weighting seems fine. For compliance we might force a hard cutoff: if format <95% fail the POC.
[02:09] Jordan Park: That makes sense. We can make format/facts a gating criterion.
[02:13] Sofia Moreno: What's the golden prompt idea?
[02:15] Lina Gomez: We recommend a set of 25-50 golden prompts - representative examples with expected outputs - that become the regression suite. These include edge cases: multi-med interactions, negations, template mismatch. For each golden prompt we store an expected canonical output (the "golden" summary) and a rubric for allowable variance.
[02:34] Ethan Li: How do you handle minor phrasing differences? Clinicians paraphrase a lot.
[02:38] Lina Gomez: We use semantic similarity thresholds on embeddings plus structured checks for critical fields. Example: doctor summary says "no penicillin allergy" vs "penicillin allergy denied" - different tokens but same meaning. Embedding similarity score above 0.88 + correct boolean for allergy passes.
[02:52] Jordan Park: Also for hallucination detection we suggested two signals: automated entity grounding plus a retrieval-augmented verification step when the model introduces facts - we can try a fast secondary retriever to check support in the source note.
[03:05] Rajiv Patel: That would be great, but retrieval has latency. We need to keep within 1.2s. Can we run the retriever only in batch/eval runs vs production?
[03:14] Lina Gomez: Exactly. For POC benchmarks we enable full verification. For production we can use lightweight checks and sampling to keep latency. During POC we want comprehensive detection to scope expected false positive/negative rates.
[03:25] Sofia Moreno: On dataset size for the bench - what do you recommend?
[03:28] Lina Gomez: For initial quality evaluation, 1,000-2,000 examples gives a stable signal. Golden prompts (25-50) are separate for regression tests. For throughput and cost benchmarking, we recommend a 5k token workload run (sampled across 2-3 hours) to estimate unit costs.
[03:44] Ethan Li: Our data volume is big; for the pilot we'll send one week of notes (~12k notes) but obviously that's too much for labelled human review. We'll sample.
[03:52] Jordan Park: Sounds good. Sampling strategy: stratified by note type and complexity, and oversample rare edge cases for golden/regression. We'll include guidance in the eval spreadsheet.
[04:02] Rajiv Patel: Can you run the initial benchmark on Redwood hosted models or do you need Dedicated?
[04:06] Lina Gomez: Hosted is fine for benchmark and quick iteration. We can evaluate economics and then recommend Dedicated or Private if isolation or throughput requirements need it.
[04:15] Sofia Moreno: For scoring approach - what thresholds would you recommend for passing?
[04:19] Jordan Park: Proposed pass criteria: format compliance >=95% (hard gate), critical entity precision >=98% on sampled set, hallucination rate <=2% for critical fields, average semantic similarity (embeddings) >=0.87, human usefulness >=4/5 on sampled clinicians. These are starting points we can tune with your stakeholders.
[04:40] Ethan Li: The 98% precision for meds seems high - our ground truth extraction isn't perfect. Can we measure both precision and recall?
[04:46] Lina Gomez: Yes we'll report precision/recall/F1 for entity checks. For gating we typically use precision to avoid false positives that could harm downstream systems.
[04:55] Rajiv Patel: Timeline? We want results in ~4 weeks.
[04:58] Jordan Park: Typical POC timeline we propose here: week 0 (this week) - agree eval plan and data exchange; week 1 - Redwood runs initial baseline on hosted models with sample data and shares results; week 2 - run golden prompts regression and clinicians do small labelled review; week 3 - run full 1k-2k benchmark with hallucination detection and cost metrics; week 4 - synthesize results, recommend next steps (Dedicated/Private or pilot). We can compress some steps if you can turn around sample data fast.
[05:24] Sofia Moreno: We can expedite data sharing but need to ensure PHI redaction/processes. Ava from security is on the call - any immediate questions Ava?
[05:32] Ava Thompson: Yes. We need to know data handling: where data lives, retention, KMS, SOC2. If using hosted endpoints, what controls on logs and PII?
[05:43] Lina Gomez: For hosted POC we can enable transient storage, disable logs retention, and sign an NDA. For production we'd recommend Private or Dedicated with customer-managed KMS. I can send the SOC2 and security docs.
[05:55] Ava Thompson: Also need audit logs and RBAC for access to outputs.
[05:59] Jordan Park: Noted. We'll include audit log options in the security pack.
[06:03] Rajiv Patel: Back to eval specifics - can you show an example of a golden prompt + rubric?
[06:07] Lina Gomez: Sure - example: Source note: "Patient reports chest pain, denies SOB, no known drug allergies, on aspirin 81mg daily. CXR normal." Golden prompt: "Summarize into JSON keys diagnosis, plan, follow_up." Expected output: JSON with diagnosis: "chest pain (likely musculoskeletal)" plan: "cardiac enzymes, discharge if stable" follow_up: "cardiology within 1 week" Variance rubric: diagnosis string can vary but must contain "chest pain" and not introduce cardiac meds unless in source. Critical fields flagged.
[06:40] Ethan Li: How do you record the rubric? Is it machine readable?
[06:44] Lina Gomez: Yes, in the eval spreadsheet we have columns for golden_output, required_entities, allowed_variance, semantic_threshold, and gating_flag. That way automation can run the checks.
[06:55] Jordan Park: We'll populate a starter spreadsheet with 25 golden prompts and the initial scoring weights.
[06:59] Sofia Moreno: For human labelling - what's the recommended reviewer panel size for Week 2?
[07:03] Lina Gomez: For a small sanity check, 5 clinicians reviewing 50 samples each gives a quick signal. For final validation we recommend 10-20 clinicians across 200 samples.
[07:13] Rajiv Patel: Cost question - what's the expected Hosted cost for the benchmark?
[07:17] Jordan Park: We'll estimate once we have exact token counts, but rough back-of-envelope: the 5k token throughput test will show per-token unit with your note length distribution; we'll provide cost scenarios for hosted vs Dedicated.
[07:27] Ethan Li: Any recommended model variants / quantization for clinical safety?
[07:30] Lina Gomez: For POC we suggest starting with our curated open model X variant (v1.3) with safety filters and then test a smaller quantized variant for cost tradeoffs. We'll report regression on quality when swapping.
[07:42] Sofia Moreno: For hallucination scoring, will you produce per-example flags and a summary rate?
[07:46] Lina Gomez: Yes - per example we output flags: format_pass boolean, meds_match boolean, allergies_match boolean, hallucination_flag boolean, semantic_score numeric, and human_label when available. Summary aggregates and percentiles included.
[07:58] Jordan Park: Good. Any blockers?
[08:00] Rajiv Patel: Security will review docs. We need NDA in place before we send any PHI.
[08:04] Jordan Park: We'll push NDA and security pack today.
[08:07] Sofia Moreno: Great. Recap and immediate next steps?
[08:10] Jordan Park: Recap: Redwood to share quality eval spreadsheet, golden prompts, and security docs by 10/17; PulseCare to share anonymized sample and redaction rules by 10/20; Redwood runs baseline hosted benchmark and returns results by 10/24; clinician sampling and human review scheduled for week 2.
[08:26] Ethan Li: Sounds good.
[08:28] Lina Gomez: I'll start assembling the golden prompts and rubrics.
[08:31] Ava Thompson: I'll coordinate security review.
[08:33] Jordan Park: Thanks everyone - we'll follow up with calendar invites for benchmark windows.
[08:38] Rajiv Patel: Thanks all.
[08:40] [meeting end]
